plan.question: Joint-project topic: label-free monitoring of industrial networks. Can site-specific baselines reduce nuisance alerts while detecting held-out operational changes? A follow-on industrial PhD could study drift-aware calibration across sites and protocols, subject to pilot evidence, supervision and funding agreements.
plan.experiment: Propose a three-month offline pilot comparing a statistical baseline and a one-class model on time-separated traffic. Hold one site out if enough sites are available. Replay agreed changes in an isolated testbed. Treat BACnet transfer as a separate experiment.
plan.metrics: Agree an alert-review budget in week 1. Proposed gate: at least 30% fewer nuisance alerts than the baseline at equal detection of the agreed replay scenarios. Report alerts/site/day, detection delay, CPU/RAM, and missed scenarios; simulated detection is not proof of real attack coverage.
plan.companyAsk: Request one engineering contact to explain maintenance events, arrange permissions and benchmark an appliance offline. Confirm availability before scheduling.
plan.researcherAsk: Invite the researcher to specify features, compare detectors and examine leakage and drift. Confirm contribution, availability and resources before assigning work.
plan.dataRequired: Request an approved traffic schema, de-identified time-stamped Modbus windows, maintenance-event labels and hardware limits. Company retains raw traffic; agree consent, access and retention before transfer.
plan.milestones: Month 1 (weeks 1–4): company clears data access; researcher delivers split protocol and statistical baseline. Month 2 (weeks 5–8): researcher compares detectors; company checks alert relevance. Month 3 (weeks 9–12): jointly test held-out windows, report resource costs and decide go/no-go with reproducible scripts.
plan.risks: Normal traffic can already contain attacks; drift may reflect maintenance. Stop if consent or de-identification is inadequate. Test BACnet separately; do not infer BACnet expertise from other protocols.
plan.meeting: Before a 45-minute meeting, request an approved trace schema, maintenance-event list and hardware limits. Engineering lead and researcher then choose sites, define nuisance alerts and name data owners. Leave with a one-page protocol, named task owners and a dated permission/budget decision before any data transfer.
plan.terms: Discuss a capped pilot budget before work; company retains raw traffic, researchers receive only approved extracts. Negotiate background IP, prototype rights and a 60-day publication review. All terms are proposed, not agreed.

plan.question: Can PCB layout rules flag actionable EMC hotspots before external testing? A follow-on industrial PhD could examine emission predictors across board families, subject to sufficient data, supervision and funding agreements.
plan.experiment: Propose a three-month feasibility pilot extracting trace/plane features and comparing a rule checklist with archived scans. Freeze rules before each held-out board; include passed boards and one prospective layout review. Output is engineering triage, not certification.
plan.metrics: Measure hotspot agreement with scans, false flags per board and engineer review time. Proposed gate: identify a plausible hotspot on every held-out failed board, with at most five actionable false flags per review; a small sample gives uncertain estimates. External lab success remains unproven.
plan.companyAsk: Request a layout engineer to annotate hotspots, assess manufacturability and reserve one review session weekly. Confirm board access and staffing.
plan.researcherAsk: Invite the researcher to map features to rules, interpret emission mechanisms and analyze held-out results. Confirm personal contribution, availability and code rights before reuse.
plan.dataRequired: Request NDA-protected Gerbers, netlists, stackups, BOMs and emission scans for passed and failed boards, with operating modes and scan conditions. Agree access and retention before transfer.
plan.milestones: Month 1 (weeks 1–4): company provides approved inventory and annotations; researcher delivers baseline checklist. Month 2 (weeks 5–8): researcher implements rules; company reviews held-out flags. Month 3 (weeks 9–12): jointly review a prospective layout and deliver scripts, evidence log and go/no-go recommendation.

Dijana Radulović
Automated PCB Layout Scoring for EMC Risk Using Feature Extraction and a Rule-Based Engine

Manual EMC design review is time-consuming and relies on reviewer expertise that varies across organisations. This paper describes a rule-based layout scoring tool that ingests Gerber files and a netlist, extracts geometric features related to emission risk, and outputs a numerical score and flagged violation list. Seventeen rules were derived from simulation studies and published guidelines, covering trace-to-plane spacing, clock trace routing

plan.question: Joint-project topic: raspberry packaging for a 14-day cold chain. Can film permeability and headspace conditions improve shelf life? A follow-on industrial PhD could model how temperature excursions and harvest-lot variation change the useful permeability range, subject to safe pilot results and supervision/funding agreements.
plan.experiment: Propose a three-month pilot randomizing trays within three harvest lots to current packaging or three candidate films. Log temperature and headspace gases; compare mold, firmness and acceptability through day 14. Obtain a food-science protocol covering sample size and safe sensory testing.
plan.metrics: Proposed gate: a candidate meets buyer-agreed mold, firmness and sensory criteria on day 14 in all pilot lots, without unsafe gas conditions. Report lot-level uncertainty and cost per pack. Day 14 is a target to test, never an outcome guaranteed by prior work.
plan.companyAsk: Request a quality contact to arrange fruit, document handling and coordinate buyer criteria. Confirm storage, measurement access and a consumables budget before starting.
plan.researcherAsk: Invite the researcher to select permeability ranges, design randomized comparisons and analyze lot variation. Confirm contribution and availability; no laboratory or supervision commitment is assumed.
plan.dataRequired: Request current film specifications, lot and harvest dates, cold-chain logs, buyer rejection thresholds and approved temperature/headspace measurements. Agree who supplies safe microbiology and sensory assessments.
plan.milestones: Month 1 (weeks 1–4): company confirms harvest windows and buyer criteria; researcher delivers reviewed protocol and film shortlist. Month 2 (weeks 5–8): jointly run three staggered lot trials. Month 3 (weeks 9–12): researcher reports uncertainty and cost; company assesses feasibility; both deliver a recommendation or documented no-go.
plan.risks: Mixed-berry results may not transfer to raspberry-only packs or fluctuating transport temperatures. Anaerobic conditions and sensory rejection can defeat longer shelf life. Do not release experimental packs for sale without the appropriate safety review.
plan.meeting: Before a 45-minute meeting, request current film specifications and one approved rejected-shipment temperature log. Quality manager and researcher agree buyer thresholds, harvest windows and who can measure gases and microbiology. Leave with a sampling plan and a dated safety/access/budget decision before sourcing films.
plan.terms: Propose a capped trial budget, company ownership of shipment records, agreed access to de-identified measurements, negotiated foreground IP and a 60-day publication review. No funding or participation is secured.
